reels.title: MCP is USB-C for AI agents

beats.say: Why can one little cable charge your phone, your laptop and your headphones?

show.sub: because everyone agreed on the shape

beats.say: Because everyone agreed on one shape. Before that, every gadget had its own charger, and every drawer was a tangle.
The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, does this for AI agents. An agent is an AI that takes actions, like running a query. MCP is the agreed plug between the agent and your tools.

A server offers three things. Tools the agent can use. Read-only information it can look at. And ready-made instructions. Build the plug once, and any compatible assistant can use it, with no custom wiring each time.

show.title: What an MCP server offers
items: Tools: things the agent can do

check.q: What is the best way to describe what MCP gives an AI agent?
opts: A faster AI model
A shared standard plug for connecting to tools and data
A database that stores agent memory
check.why: MCP is a standard interface, like USB-C. It does not make the model faster or store memory. It lets any compatible client use the same tools without custom wiring.

work: List the three tools or data sources your team would most want an assistant to reach.
Find out which of your current assistants already support MCP.

reels.title: What happens in an MCP call

beats.say: What actually happens when an agent asks your warehouse a question through MCP?
First, the client connects to the MCP server and asks what it offers. The server replies with a list: tools such as run sql, each with a name, a description, and the inputs it expects.
The model reads that list and picks a tool. The client sends the call, for example run sql with a select on yesterday's orders. The server runs it and returns rows as text.

Resources work differently. They are read-only items, like a table schema or a runbook, that the client loads into context before the model asks. Prompts are saved templates, like a standard incident triage checklist.

show.title: The other two parts
items: Resource: a schema or runbook, loaded as context
Tool: an action the model chooses to call

check.q: How does the model know which tools exist on an MCP server?
opts: The client asks the server for a list of tools with descriptions and inputs
The tools are hard-coded into the model
The model guesses names until one works
check.why: MCP clients discover tools at connection time. The server lists each tool's name, description and input shape, and the model picks from that list.

work: Write a clear one-sentence description for each tool you expose, since the model chooses by reading it.
Put your table schemas in as resources instead of letting the agent guess columns.

reels.title: Locking down a run sql tool

beats.say: An agent has a run sql tool. What is the worst that can happen?

show.text: What is the worst a run sql tool can do?
show.sub: the model decides what to call

beats.say: Plenty. It could drop a table, scan ten terabytes and burn your budget, or dump a million rows into its own context and choke. The model decides what to call, so the server must enforce the limits.
So connect with a read-only role. Cap rows, say at five hundred, and add a query timeout. Log every call with who asked and the exact text.

Never put credentials in the tool arguments or the model's context. The server holds them. Also remember that returned data can contain hidden instructions, called prompt injection, so treat rows as untrusted text.

show.title: Two more gotchas
items: Query results can carry prompt injection
Treat returned rows as untrusted text

check.q: Where should the row limit and read-only restriction be enforced?
opts: In the prompt, by asking the model to behave
In the MCP server and database role
In the user's chat message
check.why: The model's choices cannot be trusted as a safety control. A read-only database role and server-side caps hold no matter what the model tries.

work: Create a dedicated read-only warehouse role for the agent, with a query timeout and cost limit.
Log every tool call with user, timestamp and full query text.
Test your tool with a result that contains injected instructions.

reels.title: When MCP is worth it

beats.say: Should every internal system get its own MCP server?
Not automatically. MCP pays off when many clients need the same tools. One server, written once, serves your coding assistant, chat app and agent harness, instead of three custom integrations.

But every tool description costs tokens on every request. Fifty tools can eat thousands of tokens and confuse the model's choice. Keep tools few and task-shaped, like list failed runs, not raw database access.

show.title: Prompt cost grows with tool count

beats.say: For a single fixed pipeline, a plain function call or scheduled job is simpler and cheaper. Run shared servers behind central authentication, per-user roles and audit logs, so one agent cannot exceed what its user may see.

show.title: Choose deliberately
items: One fixed pipeline: use plain function calls
Always: central auth, per-user roles, audit logs

check.q: Which situation is the weakest case for building an MCP server?
opts: Three different assistants need the same warehouse tools
A single scheduled job always calls one fixed function
Many teams want a shared, audited tool catalog
check.why: MCP's value is reuse across clients and discovery. A single fixed job gains little over a direct function call, and still pays the extra moving parts.

work: Audit how many clients need each integration before deciding to wrap it in MCP.
Design tools around tasks, and keep the count small to save tokens.
Make sure the server passes the end user's identity to the warehouse so permissions follow the person.

reels.title: The builder who knows when to stop

beats.say: Would you hire a builder who never stops, never asks questions, and never shows you a receipt?

show.text: Never stops. Never asks. No receipts.

beats.say: A good builder agrees what finished means for each room. The paint is dry. The tap does not leak. Someone can check it, not just the builder's word.
They also have a budget. If the bathroom costs double, they stop and call you. And if the same pipe bursts three times, they ask rather than guess.
At the end, they hand over receipts and photos. An agent doing data work needs the same four habits: a clear finish line, a budget, asking for help, and proof.

show.title: Four habits of a trusted agent

check.q: In the builder story, what should happen when the same pipe bursts a third time?
opts: Try a fourth fix quietly
Stop and ask the owner
Skip the room and report it done
Double the budget
check.why: Repeated failure means guessing is unlikely to help. Stopping and asking saves money and avoids hidden damage.

work: Write down what done means for your next automated task before you start it.
Decide who an agent should ask when it gets stuck.
Ask for proof, not just a summary, the next time an automated tool reports success.

reels.title: Done, budget, escalate, prove

beats.say: Your agent has forty tables to migrate. How does it know when one is truly done?

show.sub: Not when the agent says so

beats.say: Each table gets a definition of done, checked by code. Tests pass, row counts match the source exactly, and null checks stay clean. The agent's opinion does not count.

Each table gets a budget, say two dollars and twenty tool calls. The whole run gets two hundred dollars. If the same error appears three times, the agent writes its question to the progress file and stops.
At the end it reports cost per finished table, and every claim links to a log line, a query result or a test output.

show.title: Report with evidence
items: Claim links to a log line

check.q: Who or what should decide that a migrated table is done?
opts: The agent's own summary
Automated checks such as tests and row counts
The cheapest run
Whichever table finishes first
check.why: Code checks are repeatable and cannot be talked around. The agent's own statement is a claim, not evidence.

work: Give every sub-task a pass or fail check such as a row count comparison.
Set a per-task and per-run spend cap in your agent harness.
Make the agent write blocked questions to a progress file after three identical errors.

reels.title: How agents fool you by accident

beats.say: An agent says all forty tables pass. Why might you still not trust it?
Because it can cheat without meaning to. Stuck on a failing test, it may loosen the test. So keep the checks in files the agent cannot edit, and run them from outside.
The three strikes rule has a gap. An error message with a changing timestamp looks new each time. Strip ids and times, then count the cleaned signature.
Row counts alone can match while values are wrong, so add checksums on key columns. And evidence must be captured by the harness, not typed by the agent, or it can invent a log line.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Counts match, values wrong: add checksums
Agent never writes its own proof

check.q: An agent keeps hitting an error whose message includes a new timestamp each time. What goes wrong with a naive three-strikes rule?
opts: It stops too early
Each error looks different, so the counter never reaches three
It counts the errors twice
It deletes the progress file
check.why: Raw messages differ, so no single message repeats. Normalize by stripping ids and times, then count the cleaned signature.

work: Store tests and checks where the agent has read-only access.
Normalize error messages before counting repeats.
Add checksum comparisons on key columns, not only row counts.

reels.title: When not to trust an agent

beats.say: When should you not hand a data task to an autonomous agent?

show.text: When should you say no to an agent?

beats.say: When you cannot write a check for done. If correctness is a judgment call, like a metric definition, the agent will produce confident output nobody can verify. Use a person, or a plain script.
Budgets are a trade. Set them too tight and the agent stops on tasks a human finds easy. Too loose and one loop burns a week of spend overnight. Start tight, and tune from cost per finished item.
Keep production writes behind human approval, and let agents work in a sandbox. Escalation is cheap. A wrong guess in production is not.

check.q: Which task is the worst fit for a fully autonomous agent?
opts: Backfilling a table, with row counts and checksums to compare
Renaming columns, with a test suite covering them
Deciding what the company's active customer metric should mean
Fixing a failing unit test in a sandbox
check.why: A metric definition is a judgment call with no code check for correct, so the output cannot be verified. The other tasks have automated pass or fail checks.

work: Before adopting an agent for a task, ask whether code can verify done; if not, keep a human in charge.
Start with tight budgets and loosen them using cost per finished item.
Route all production writes through human approval and let the agent work in a sandbox.

reels.title: The builder with a clipboard

beats.say: Picture a brilliant builder who forgets everything each night. How do they finish a six month renovation?
You leave a clipboard. One page is the plan: every job, and whether it is done. Another page is a diary: what happened today, and what comes next.
Each morning the builder reads the clipboard, does one job, checks it works, then ticks it off. If the builder quits, a stranger reads the same clipboard and carries on.
An AI agent working on data is that builder. Its memory, called the context window, fills up, so files become its memory.

show.text: The clipboard survives. The builder does not.
show.sub: Context window = what the agent can hold in mind at once

check.q: In the builder story, what lets a stranger take over mid-renovation?
opts: The builder's memory of yesterday
The clipboard with the plan and diary
A bigger toolbox
check.why: The state lives in written files, not in anyone's head, so anyone can pick up from them.

work: Write down where your current long task keeps its state. If the answer is only chat history, move it to a file.
Try handing a half-done task to a colleague using only notes, and see what is missing.

reels.title: Forty models, one step at a time

beats.say: How does an agent migrate forty dbt models when one context window holds maybe five?

show.sub: One context window cannot hold the whole job

beats.say: First, an initialiser session writes the plan file: forty rows, each marked todo. It also sets up the environment and never touches a model.
Then a worker starts fresh. It reads the plan, takes the first todo, and changes just that one model. It runs the build and a row count check against the old output.

If it passes, it commits to git and marks the row done. It adds a line to the progress file: what changed, what is next, and a link to the test result. Then the session ends and the next worker repeats.

chip.text: A crash loses at most one step

check.q: Why does a worker change only one model per step?
opts: It can be verified, committed and reverted on its own
dbt only allows one model per run
It makes the plan file shorter
check.why: Small verified steps make each checkpoint clean, so a bad step is reverted alone and a crash loses very little.

work: Split your next big migration into a plan file with one row per model and a status column.
Define the check that must pass before any row can be marked done, such as row counts or a data diff.

reels.title: Killed mid-backfill

beats.say: You kill the agent halfway through a backfill. What happens when a new session starts?

show.sub: It should continue from the files without redoing work

beats.say: If the work was committed after each step, you lose at most one step. But a crash can land between the change and the tick, so the plan says todo for something that is half done.
So steps must be safe to repeat. An append that ran twice doubles a month of rows. Use overwrite by partition, or merge on a key, so a rerun gives the same result.
Also, workers must only mark done after a check passes, and the plan should be edited by status only. Otherwise a tired agent rewrites the plan and quietly drops hard tasks.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Done only after a passing check
Edit status, never the task list
On start, compare plan against git and the warehouse

check.q: A worker crashes after loading day 14 but before marking it done. What makes the restart safe?
opts: Trusting the plan file, since it is the source of truth
Loading day 14 with an idempotent overwrite or merge
Deleting the progress file and starting over
check.why: The plan may be one step behind reality, so repeating the step must give the same result. Overwrite by partition or merge on a key does that.

work: Review each backfill step and make it idempotent: overwrite a partition or merge on a key, never plain append.
Add a start-up check that compares the plan with git history and the target tables before the worker picks a task.

reels.title: When not to use a long-running agent

beats.say: When is a long-running agent the wrong tool?

show.text: Not every long job needs an agent

beats.say: Every fresh session pays to reread the plan and progress. If the job fits one window, or is the same mechanical edit forty times, a script or an orchestrator is cheaper and more predictable.

chip.text: Pay for judgement only where needed

beats.say: Use agents where each item needs judgement, like odd SQL dialect quirks. Keep the plan small: at thousands of items, move it to a table and let workers fetch just the next row.

show.title: Scale limits
items: Agents earn their cost on varied items
A plan file of thousands of rows bloats every session
Move it to a table and fetch the next row

beats.say: Parallel workers need a claim step, or two will take the same item. And add a human review gate before anything touches production, because commits protect code, not warehouse data.

check.q: Which job is the best fit for a long-running agent harness?
opts: Renaming one column in 40 models with a single regex
Migrating 40 models whose SQL quirks each differ and need testing
Running a nightly load that never changes
check.why: Agents pay off when each item needs judgement. Identical mechanical edits and stable loads are cheaper and safer with a script or orchestrator.

work: Before building a harness, ask whether a deterministic script covers 80 percent of the items, and give the agent only the rest.
Put a human approval gate in front of any step that writes to production tables, and estimate per-session token cost first.

reels.title: The night-shift mechanic

beats.say: What if the person woken at three in the morning already had the answer waiting?

show.sub: What if the answer is already waiting?

beats.say: Picture a night-shift mechanic at a factory. An alarm goes off. She reads the last lines of the machine's log, checks what changed yesterday, and tests her guess before touching anything.
She may write a repair note, but she cannot press the big red button herself. A manager must sign first.
An on-call data agent works the same way. A pipeline fails, it reads the error, investigates, and hands you a report with evidence and a proposed fix. You approve.

show.title: The on-call data agent
items: Agent reads the error and investigates
Report with evidence and proposed fix

check.q: In the mechanic analogy, what is the agent not allowed to do on its own?
opts: Read the log
Apply the fix without human approval
Check recent changes
Test its guess
check.why: The agent investigates and proposes, but a human signs off before any change goes live, like the manager in the analogy.

work: List which pipeline failures wake you up most often.
Write down who would approve a fix if an agent proposed one.
Note what a good incident report must contain: cause, evidence, proposed fix.

reels.title: From failed task to proposed fix

beats.say: How does an agent turn a failed Airflow task into a ready fix in about five minutes?
The failure triggers it. First it reads only the last two hundred lines of the task log, because the error lives at the end and the full log would waste tokens.

chip.text: Tail only: cheaper, error is at the end

beats.say: Next it forms a guess, say a renamed column. It gathers evidence: the DAG code, the git log of recent changes, and a read-only query against the warehouse to verify the column is really gone.
Confident? It calls propose patch, which writes a branch and a diff but cannot merge. Then it posts the report and asks a human to approve.

check.q: Why does the agent run a read-only query before proposing a patch?
opts: To speed up the DAG
To verify its hypothesis with evidence instead of trusting a guess
To fix the data directly
To avoid reading the log
check.why: The log and git history suggest a cause; a verifying query confirms it, so the report rests on evidence rather than a plausible story.

work: Give your agent a log tool that returns the tail, with an option to page back.
Make run_sql use a read-only warehouse role.
Require every report to include the evidence that confirmed the cause.

reels.title: Confident and wrong

beats.say: Why does an on-call agent sometimes sound sure and still be wrong?

Because a log tail shows the symptom, not always the cause. An out-of-memory kill just says killed, and a late upstream looks like an empty table. So the rule is: no verifying query, no confident claim.
It also needs stop rules. If the budget runs out or two steps add no new evidence, it posts what it knows and the open question, instead of looping and burning money.

show.title: Stop rules
items: Budget cap on steps, tokens and queries
No new evidence in two steps: stop
Post findings and the open question

beats.say: Test it by injecting ten known failures, like schema change, bad credentials, and duplicate rerun. Score correct cause, cited evidence, zero unsafe actions, plus minutes and cost.

check.q: The log shows only the word Killed. What should the agent do?
opts: Declare out of memory and propose more memory
Gather evidence, such as memory limits and run history, before claiming a cause
Rerun the task repeatedly
Stay silent
check.why: Killed is a symptom with several possible causes. The agent should verify before claiming, or report the open question.

work: Build an injected-failure test set before trusting the agent.
Add a hard budget and a no-progress stop to the loop.
Fail the evaluation on any unsafe action, whatever the accuracy.

reels.title: When not to put an agent on call

beats.say: When should you not put an agent on call?

show.text: Not every alert needs an agent
show.sub: match the tool to the failure

beats.say: If a failure has a known fix, like a transient timeout, a plain retry rule is cheaper, faster, and predictable. Save the agent for the unfamiliar failures that need investigation.

chip.text: Cheap rules first, agent for the unknown

beats.say: Safety belongs in the tools, not the prompt. No merge permission, read-only credentials, and a hard cap on tokens and queries per incident.

show.title: Safety lives in the tools
items: Hard cap on tokens and queries

beats.say: At scale, one broken upstream can fail two hundred tasks. Group alerts by root cause first, or you pay for two hundred investigations. Compare cost per incident with engineer minutes saved.

check.q: What is the strongest way to keep the agent from merging bad code?
opts: Tell it in the prompt not to merge
Give its tools no merge permission
Ask it to be careful
Review its logs weekly
check.why: Prompts can be ignored or manipulated. A permission boundary in the tool makes the unsafe action impossible.

work: Route known failure patterns to retry rules before the agent.
Group alerts by root cause before triggering investigations.
Track cost per incident against engineer minutes saved.

reels.title: The night caretaker story

beats.say: An interviewer asks: have you built an agent that runs in production? What do you say?

Think of a night caretaker in a big building. An alarm rings at three in the morning. The caretaker checks the gauges, reads the log book, and leaves a note for the boss. But the caretaker cannot open the vault.

chip.text: Can look and report, cannot open the vault

beats.say: Your on-call agent is the same. When a data pipeline breaks, it reads logs, finds the likely cause, and proposes a fix. A human approves anything risky.
So tell it as a story: the problem, the design, the safety limits, the results in numbers, the cost, and one mistake you found and fixed.

check.q: In the caretaker analogy, what does the locked vault stand for?
opts: The agent's logs
Actions the agent may not take without a human
The cost of each incident
The eval set
check.why: The vault is the risky action, like changing production data. The agent can investigate and propose, but a human approves.

work: Write your agent story in six lines: problem, design, guardrails, numbers, cost, one failure.
Say it out loud in under two minutes.

reels.title: Inside the on-call harness

beats.say: What does the harness around your on-call agent actually look like?
An alert fires. The harness gives the agent only read tools: logs, table metadata, lineage, and recent code changes. It caps the loop at twelve steps, so the agent cannot wander forever.
It returns a diagnosis with evidence, and a proposed fix as a pull request. It never applies the fix itself.
To measure it, replay sixty past incidents. Say it names the right root cause in forty-five. That is seventy-five percent, a number you can defend.
Cost matters too: about forty cents per incident, against forty minutes of an engineer's night.

check.q: Why replay past incidents to evaluate the agent?
opts: It makes the agent faster
It gives a measurable accuracy number against known answers
It removes the need for guardrails
It lowers token cost
check.why: Past incidents have known root causes, so you can score the agent's diagnosis and report a defensible percentage.

work: Collect 30 to 60 resolved incidents with their true root causes.
Log steps, tokens and cost for every agent run.

reels.title: The failure you can tell

beats.say: Interviewers love one question: tell me about a time your agent failed.

Here is mine. A job died with an out of memory error, and the agent blamed it and proposed more memory. The real cause was a schema change hours earlier that exploded a join. The agent trusted the last error line, not the first.
The harness fix: a tool that returns the first error in the run, plus a rule that every diagnosis must quote its evidence. We added that incident to the eval set, so it can never quietly return.
Also remember logs are untrusted text. Data could contain instructions, so the agent keeps read-only credentials.

check.q: What was the best fix for an agent that trusted the last error line?
opts: Use a bigger model
Add more memory to the job
Give it a first-error tool and require quoted evidence
Remove the agent from on-call
check.why: The problem was the harness, not the model. Better tools and an evidence rule fix the behavior, and an eval case prevents regression.

work: Review your last 10 wrong diagnoses and group them by cause.
Turn each failure into a permanent eval case.

reels.title: When not to build the agent

beats.say: When would you not build an on-call agent?
If you get ten incidents a month, a good runbook and a dashboard win. The agent costs more to build and evaluate than it saves.
If most failures are the same three patterns, write plain scripts for them. They are cheaper, faster, and fully predictable. Keep the agent for the long tail of odd failures.
At two hundred incidents a month, forty cents each is eighty dollars. That is trivial next to engineer time. The real cost is maintaining the evals.

show.sub: The real cost is eval upkeep

beats.say: Widen autonomy slowly: suggest, then approve, then auto-run only reversible fixes.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason to use scripts instead of an agent for some incidents?
opts: Agents cannot read logs
Scripts are cheaper, faster and predictable for known repeated failures
Scripts never need maintenance
Agents cost thousands per incident
check.why: Known repeated patterns suit deterministic automation. Reserve the agent for varied failures where flexibility pays.

work: Rank your incidents by pattern and script the top three.
Estimate monthly volume times cost per incident, plus eval upkeep, before building.

reels.title: Trying a new agent tool like a new hire

beats.say: Every week there is a new agent tool. How do you decide which one deserves your trust?

Think of hiring a temp worker. Before handing over the keys, you ask four things. What problem do they take off my plate? What do they cost for each job done well? Can I test them on my own tasks by Friday? And what new risk walks in with them?

show.title: Four hiring questions
items: What does it cost per job done well?
Can I test it in a day?
What new risk comes with it?

beats.say: A shiny tool that fails your test is just a noisy coworker. A boring one that passes is a good hire.

check.q: A new agent product has an impressive demo. What is the best next step?
opts: Run it on your own tasks and measure the result
Adopt it because the vendor is well known
Wait a year until every team uses it
Trust the demo if it handled one hard case
check.why: A demo shows the best case. Only your own tasks show whether the tool removes your problem at a cost and risk you accept.

work: Write down the four judging questions and use them in your next tool review.
Collect ten real tasks from your team to serve as a quick trial set.
Note the cost and the new risk for any tool before approving a pilot.

reels.title: Server-side threads: send only what is new

beats.say: Your agent is on turn forty. Why is it still resending turns one to thirty-nine?

Normally the API remembers nothing. Each call carries the full history, so the payload grows every turn and you pay to process it again. With server-side threads, now in beta, the conversation lives on the server. Your agent sends only the new message.
So turn forty sends one small message, not forty. That means less data on the wire and less code to manage history.
One catch: the thread expires after five idle minutes.

check.q: What changes when an agent uses a server-side thread?
opts: Each turn sends only the new messages
The model gets a larger memory inside its weights
History never expires as long as the key is valid
The agent no longer needs tool results in context
check.why: The server stores the conversation, so each turn adds only new messages. It is storage of the history, not a change to the model, and it expires when idle.

work: Measure the payload size per turn in one of your agents before and after threads.
Check which of your agents pause for more than five minutes.
Keep threads in beta use behind a flag so you can fall back to full history.

reels.title: Locking a leaked key to your own runners

beats.say: If an agent key leaks, can a stranger use it from anywhere?
Not with IP allowlisting, now in beta in the Claude Console. You list up to one thousand addresses or ranges. Any API request from outside that list is refused.
So you list your own runners, the servers where agents run. A thief who copies the key from a log still gets refused, because their address is not on the list.
It limits the damage but does not replace rotating keys. And if your runner addresses change, update the list, or your own agents get locked out.

check.q: What does IP allowlisting on an agent key protect against?
opts: A copied key being used from outside your addresses
Prompt injection inside documents the agent reads
The agent writing wrong data to a table
Model errors caused by long conversations
check.why: The allowlist refuses requests from unlisted addresses, so a stolen key is useless elsewhere. It does not address what the agent does with its legitimate access.

work: List the egress addresses of every runner that calls the API.
Add address changes to your deployment checklist so the list stays current.
Keep rotating keys even after the allowlist is on.

reels.title: When the thread expires, the log saves you

beats.say: Your agent waits twenty minutes for a warehouse job to finish. What happens to its memory?
The server thread expired after five idle minutes. The next call finds nothing, and the agent wakes up with amnesia.
So a long running agent keeps its own log: every message and tool result, written to storage you control. On resume, rebuild from the log, start a fresh thread, and carry on.

steps.label: Write each turn to your log

beats.say: Treat the server thread as a cache, not as the record. A cache can vanish. A log is the truth.

check.q: An agent sleeps for an hour between steps. What is the safest design?
opts: Keep its own log and rebuild the thread on resume
Send a ping each minute so the thread never expires
Store everything only in the server thread
Restart the whole task from step one every time
check.why: Threads are a cache that can expire. A log you own lets the agent rebuild context and continue exactly where it stopped.

work: Add a durable log of messages and tool results to every long-running agent.
Test your agent by forcing a thread expiry mid-task.
Make resume idempotent so a replayed step does not repeat a write.

reels.title: Self-healing pipelines: score them on your failures

beats.say: A vendor says its agent fixes broken pipelines by itself. How do you know it is not just guessing?
Snowflake's coding agent reads a failure, traces the likely cause, and proposes a fix for a person to review. It is the on-call agent idea, sold as a product.

Do not trust the demo. Inject your own failures: a renamed column, a late file, a permissions change, a bad type. Run each one and score three things. Did it find the real cause? Was the fix correct? Did the change stay under review?
A confident wrong diagnosis is worse than none, because it wastes the on-call engineer's first hour.

check.q: How should you evaluate a self-healing pipeline agent?
opts: Inject known failures and score cause, fix and review
Count how many alerts it closes each week
Read the vendor's list of supported errors
Run it unattended and watch for complaints
check.why: Known injected failures give a ground truth, so you can score whether the cause and fix are right. Closed alerts or silence do not show correctness.

work: Build a set of ten injected failures from your own past incidents.
Score cause found, fix correct, and time saved for each run.
Keep a human review step before any fix reaches production.

reels.title: Routing models: cheap only if it holds up

beats.say: A router sends easy requests to a cheap model. Where does the saving turn into a loss?
Cortex AI Gateway's automatic model tiers, in private preview, pick a model for each request. If the cheap tier handles most traffic, the bill drops fast.
But a cheap model that fails costs twice: the failed try, then the retry on the strong model, plus the human who cleans up. So measure cost per successful task, not cost per call.
Build an eval set from real requests. Run it through each tier. Turn the router on only where the cheap tier matches the quality. Re-run it whenever the tiers change.

check.q: Why measure cost per successful task when judging a router?
opts: Failures add retries and cleanup that erase savings
Cheaper tiers always raise the price per token
Successful tasks use fewer tokens than failed ones
The router charges extra for every routed request
check.why: A cheap tier that fails triggers retries and human fixes, so the true price is spent per success, not per call.

work: Build an eval set of real requests before turning on any router.
Track cost per successful task by tier on a dashboard.
Re-run the eval whenever the provider changes the tiers.

reels.title: Always-on agents with your rights

beats.say: An agent that runs at three in the morning, with your permissions, and asks only for sign off. Is that a feature or a risk?
Snowflake's async agent API and scheduled automations are generally available. Always-on bots are coming in preview. They act with the user's rights, so they can touch everything that user can.
That is the trade. You gain work done while people sleep. You risk a mistake with full rights and one approval click that nobody reads.
Prefer a dedicated service role with narrow rights, limits on where its key works, and approvals that show the exact change. Adopt when the problem removed is bigger than the new risk.

check.q: What is the safest way to run an always-on agent?
opts: Give it a narrow service role and show exact changes
Let it use the owner's full rights to avoid blockers
Approve everything in bulk once each week
Skip approvals once it has run well for a month
check.why: Narrow rights cap the damage of any mistake, and approvals that show the exact change keep the human check meaningful.

work: Create a dedicated low-privilege role for each scheduled agent.
Make approval requests show the exact SQL or change, not a summary.
Review what each agent could touch before moving from preview to production.

reels.title: The editor and six reporters

beats.say: Would you ask one person to read six books, or give one book to each of six people?
Picture an editor with six reporters. The editor splits the story, and each reporter works alone in their own notebook. Then the editor stitches the pieces into one article.
That is a multi-agent system. The editor is the orchestrator. The reporters are subagents. Each starts with a clean, empty notebook, which we call a fresh context.

show.title: The vocabulary
items: Orchestrator: the editor who splits and merges
Subagent: a reporter doing one part
Fresh context: a clean, empty notebook

beats.say: It shines when the pieces are independent, like six sources. But for one tightly linked piece, like a single paragraph, splitting just causes confusion, and you pay six wages.

check.q: Which job suits an orchestrator with subagents best?
opts: Rewriting one tangled SQL model
Summarising six independent documents
Fixing a single line of a query
Writing one paragraph that builds on itself
check.why: Independent pieces can be handled separately and merged. Tightly linked work loses context when split.

work: List a recent task and mark whether its parts were independent or linked.
Try splitting one research task by source and compare with doing it in one go.

reels.title: Ten files in one minute

beats.say: How do you review ten files in one minute instead of ten?
The orchestrator reads the task and splits it into ten independent jobs, one per file. It starts ten subagents. Each gets only its file and instructions, in a fresh context.
They run in parallel, so ten one-minute reviews finish in about a minute, not ten. Each returns a short summary, not its whole working.

The orchestrator merges the ten summaries into one report. The catch is cost. Every subagent pays to load its own context, so total tokens, the units you are billed for, can be three to five times higher.

check.q: Why does a multi-agent run usually cost more tokens than one agent?
opts: Subagents refuse to share a model
Each subagent loads its own context and instructions
Parallel runs are billed at a higher rate
The orchestrator re-reads every file ten times
check.why: Every fresh context must be loaded and paid for, so the repeated overhead multiplies total tokens, even though time drops.

work: Estimate tokens for one agent versus N subagents before choosing a design.
Make subagents return short summaries so the merge step stays cheap.

reels.title: Where handoffs break

beats.say: Why do five agents editing one SQL model often do worse than one?

Because a handoff is lossy. A subagent only knows what the orchestrator wrote in its brief. If the join logic lives in another agent's head, it guesses. Two agents may rename the same column differently, and the merge breaks.
Summaries lose detail too. If a subagent reports all clear, the orchestrator cannot see what it skipped. Errors also compound: a wrong early answer gets passed on as fact.

show.title: Failure modes
items: A wrong early answer spreads as fact
Cost grows with every retry loop

beats.say: Safer rules: give subagents read-only or separate outputs, set a budget on tokens and retries, and have a reviewer agent with a different prompt check the result.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Read-only or separate outputs per subagent
Hard budget on tokens and retries
Reviewer agent with a different prompt

check.q: A subagent reports that its file looks fine. What is the main risk?
opts: The summary may hide what it skipped
Subagents cannot read files
The orchestrator will run out of models
It will always be faster than checking
check.why: The orchestrator sees only the summary, so omissions are invisible. A reviewer with a different prompt can catch them.

work: Give each subagent its own output file so edits never collide.
Add a reviewer step and a token and retry limit to any agent loop.

reels.title: When to say no to multi-agent

beats.say: When should an architect refuse a multi-agent design?

Start with one agent. Add more only when work is independent and parallel, like researching six sources. If steps depend on each other, a fixed pipeline or one agent with good tools is cheaper and easier to debug.
When you do split, mix models. Cheap small models handle search and summarising, where volume is high. Spend a large model only on the decisions, like which fix to apply.
Measure before you commit. Compare tokens, latency and error rate against the single agent baseline. If you pay four times the tokens for a minute saved, it is not worth it.

check.q: Which design is the best use of mixed model sizes?
opts: Large model for every search, small model for decisions
Small models for search and summaries, large model for decisions
One large model per file, no orchestrator
Small models for everything including final decisions
check.why: High-volume low-risk steps go to cheap models, and the expensive model is kept for the few judgments that matter.

work: Benchmark a single-agent baseline before approving any multi-agent design.
Route search and summarising to a small model and keep decisions on a large one.
